articles.title: US entrepreneur Morissa Schwartz used AI assistants to make her working day easier, but her to-do list grew to 156 tasks; she now caps it at 25 and says completing work matters more than planning it
articles.summary: Every few weeks, another AI assistant promises to take a task off your plate.
articles.body: Every few weeks, another AI assistant promises to take a task off your plate. The promises are tempting: it can draft the email, sort the inbox and plan the week. The question is no longer whether these tools can do the work. It’s whether they are lightening the load or quietly adding to it. Morissa Schwartz, an entrepreneur, author and AI strategist, recently discovered just how easily an attempt to improve productivity can turn into another job. “I believe in AI. But my AI assistant gave me more work than it could finish. I opened my daily to-do list and found 156 items,” she wrote in Fortune.Despite having AI assistants to manage her workload, she found her daily to-do list flooded with 156 items. Instead of making her work easier, her AI assistant had created a growing list of tasks. The reminders and follow-ups threatened to overwhelm the very system designed to keep her organised.Her to-do list hit 156 itemsMorissa Schwartz explained how asking AI to help with a project often leads to a plan, which is then followed by a checklist and eventually a series of additional tasks. Though each may appear useful individually, the growing list can turn productivity management into another task.She isn’t against technology. Her complaint is that an assistant can produce work faster than anyone can finish it. Her fix was to cap her daily list at roughly 25 meaningful entries and ask a sharper question about every task: what would ‘done’ look like to the person who asked for it? In her profession as a publisher, that would mean a finished draft. If the request was to pitch it, done means the pitch was sent.She revealed how she retrained her AI assistants. “Here are the changes I’m making. First, I want a daily list that reflects available capacity. For assistant execution, I’m aiming for roughly 25 meaningful entries on a weekday, while preserving real deadlines and necessary daily operations. The number is a working limit for my system, rather than a productivity prescription for everyone.” Its purpose was to force her system to prioritise tasks instead of treating everything as equally urgent. “If everything is due today, the list has stopped helping me decide what to do today.”Flexible work also moves into a backlog with a regular checkpoint. Items waiting on someone else get a waiting status rather than a place at the top. Related steps, such as research, outreach and follow-ups for a single campaign, are grouped under one execution item. The details stay available, but they stop competing for attention. “A genuine deadline deserves space that has not already been occupied by 40 vaguely urgent reminders,” she wrote.Proof before checkmarksHer second rule is to group related tasks under one main item instead of listing each one separately. For instance, research, outreach and follow-ups for a campaign could be managed under a single task, keeping the to-do list shorter and easier to manage without losing important details.Third is, of course, evidence. If the assistant says an email went out, she wants to see it in the sent folder. If something was published, she wants the live link. If a file was delivered, she wants the usable file and a record of the delivery. It’s not that she does not ‘trust’ her agents. Rather, she believes evidence matters. “That proof also helps prevent duplicate work. A system that remembers what actually happened can stop proposing the same action with slightly different punctuation,” she wrote.Fourth, a ‘blocker’ needs to be specific. “‘Unable to complete’ gives me another mystery to manage. ‘The form requires an answer only you can provide’ gives me a decision. ‘This browser session cannot access the account’ identifies an access problem,” she said. She wanted the AI to explain clearly why a task could not be completed, whether it needed her input or had an access issue. This would help her solve the problem quickly without delaying other tasks.Finally, Schwartz measures outcomes. How many pitches went out? Which replies still need an answer? What was accepted? Which deliverables reached the client? What remains unfinished? “I care about those numbers because they describe the work I was trying to accomplish. A magnificent list of possible actions describes the system’s imagination,” she said.Schwartz is not arguing that AI should do less. She still wants an assistant. What she wants is one that rewards finishing, checks its own claims and says plainly what is left. By her measure, a good day has fewer items on the list and a clearer record of what was sent, published or delivered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Federal authorities have arrested more than two dozen foreign nationals in California for allegedly registering and voting illegally in US elections, as the Trump administration intensifies its efforts to crack down on noncitizen voting ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.According to the Associated Press, the arrests were made on Monday as part of a statewide operation dubbed “Operation Protect the Vote”. The Justice Department said all those arrested were lawful permanent residents, but not US citizens eligible to vote in federal elections.The accused face charges including making false statements on naturalisation applications and submitting fraudulent voter registrations.The crackdown comes despite data indicating that noncitizen voting is extremely rare in the US, difficult to establish and has not been shown to have changed the outcome of elections, AP reported.The arrests also mark a fresh escalation in the dispute between the Trump administration and California over voter registration records and election procedures.California at centre of voter roll disputeThe Justice Department has made investigating noncitizen voting a priority this year, seeking detailed voter information from states, including dates of birth, addresses, driving licence numbers and partial Social Security numbers.Before Monday’s arrests, federal prosecutors had charged around 90 people with various election-related offences this year, including about 50 accused of voting as noncitizens. The US had more than 227 million registered voters during the 2024 presidential election.California, a heavily Democratic state, has emerged as a major focus of the administration’s efforts. Although it is not generally considered a key battleground in presidential elections, several competitive congressional races in the state could influence which party controls the US House of Representatives for the remaining two years of President Donald Trump’s term.More than 23 million people are registered to vote in California.Last week, the Justice Department sued the state, seeking to prevent officials from counting mail-in ballots cast by people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status is verified.The lawsuit followed a dispute over a password-protected thumb drive containing a list of 20,000 names. Federal officials claimed the individuals were likely noncitizens who had been sent ballots for the November 3 election.California officials did not meet a 48-hour deadline set by the federal government to review the list. The state's secretary of state said the administration had provided no evidence to substantiate its claims, AP reported.California sends mail-in ballots to all registered voters.Justice Department warns election workersThe dispute intensified on Friday when the Justice Department warned California election officials that knowingly processing or counting ballots cast by noncitizens could expose them to federal investigations and potential prosecution.In a letter addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said noncitizen voting in federal elections was a federal crime and warned that knowingly facilitating such conduct was also unlawful.The letter further cautioned that election workers who knowingly counted ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens could risk being treated as aiding and abetting a federal offence.The warning was also sent to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, placing state and local election officials on notice less than three weeks before Election Day.Responding to the letter, Logan said his office remained focused on ensuring a fair and secure election, noting that Election Day was just 18 days away.He said the Justice Department had chosen to pursue its unverified claims through litigation and added that the matter was best addressed in court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
articles.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.
articles.body:
More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.

The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".

The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".

Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.

At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.

However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.

The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls

Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.

A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.

The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.

In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.summary: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.
articles.body:
As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.

But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.

And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.

Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.

Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.

Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack

What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car

Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.

In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.

Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.

According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.

"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.

Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.

But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.

"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.

"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."

And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.

Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.

"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.

And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.

"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.

There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.

It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.

Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.

"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.

"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title: Christiane Amanpour: CNN reporter and anchor to leave network after 43 years
articles.summary: The network's chief international anchor has covered wars including Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran.
articles.body:
CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.

"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" Amanpour said in a statement.

The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".

CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".

Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.

She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.

In a memo to staff on Monday, Thompson wrote: "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months.

"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.

"In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship," he added.

In her own statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews."

Amanpour reflected on her "very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between".

"It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she continued, "as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour."

articles.title: How HSBC’s Sharia fund invested millions in Israeli war-linked firms
articles.summary: HSBC bought $130m in shares in firms tied to Israel’s military, in breach of Islamic law compliance requirements.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom’s biggest so-called Sharia-compliant fund spent more than $130 million to buy shares in several companies linked to the Israeli military amid an ongoing genocide in Gaza, pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and occupation of southern Lebanon.

HSBC, Europe’s second-largest bank, invested the funds through its Islamic Global Equity Index Fund in companies linked to Israel’s military supply chain – from components used in weapons to technology and equipment with military applications.

The firms range from US tech giant Palantir to the world’s second-largest arms company, RTX.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,300 Palestinians since October 2023, including nearly 1,500 killed since a “ceasefire” was agreed upon last year.

Israel’s war, which has devastated the Palestinian enclave of 2.3 million people, has drawn global condemnation.

Investments by the HSBC fund raise several questions, including: can money marketed as being compliant with Islamic law flow into companies linked to the Israeli military?

What is HSBC’s Islamic Global Equity Index Fund?

With more than $8bn in assets, HSBC’s Islamic fund channels the savings of investors, expected to be predominantly Muslim, into global equities screened against Islamic financial principles.

The bank’s website for the fund says it delivers “both investment returns and better outcomes for society as a whole”, describing its Sharia philosophy as “ethical investments that enhance society”.

It is supposed to exclude businesses and financial practices deemed forbidden under its Islamic law screening rules, with oversight from a Sharia committee.

HSBC says it has an independent Sharia Committee consisting of two internationally renowned Islamic scholars overseeing investment in the fund “to ensure compliance with Islamic principles”.

Under its own Sharia philosophy that dictates the fund’s investments, as reviewed by Al Jazeera, HSBC says it ensures that a “company has no significant exposure to non-permissible revenue sources such as selling goods or services related to … weapons”.

Wahyu Jatmiko, a lecturer at the University of Southampton Business School, with a focus on Islamic finance, told Al Jazeera that there are “strong grounds to criticise HSBC’s governance, transparency, and handling of investors’ ethical expectations.”

“The strongest concern is the apparent tension between its stated restrictions and the reported investments,” he said.

“This should also be a lesson for the whole Islamic finance industry. The ‘Sharia’ label should mean something; it carries expectations about investing differently and realising the higher ethical objectives of Islamic law,” Jatmiko told Al Jazeera.

To which companies did HSBC channel its Sharia-compliant fund?

An analysis of the HSBC Sharia-compliant fund’s activities in the first half of 2026 shows that the bank purchased shares in at least five companies linked to the Israeli military’s wars in the Middle East.

These purchases were first reported by Middle East Eye and Hyphen news publications.

Palantir Technologies, a US data analytics and artificial intelligence company, has faced scrutiny over its support for Israel’s military. In January 2024, the company announced a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defence to support “war-related missions” and held a board meeting in Tel Aviv in solidarity with Israel.

Hyphen reported last week that HSBC’s fund purchased $38.3m worth of shares in the US tech giant.

Palantir’s software integrates large volumes of data to help military and intelligence agencies analyse information and make operational decisions.

A United Nations report in June 2025 identified Palantir Technologies as expanding its support to the Israeli military since the start of the Gaza war. The report said there were “reasonable grounds” to believe the company provided automatic predictive policing technology used for automated decision-making in the battlefield, to process data and generate lists of targets, including through artificial intelligence systems such as “Lavender”, “Gospel” and “Where’s Daddy?”

The US military also reportedly relied on Palantir’s systems in falsely identifying a school in the Iranian city of Minab as a target in a strike that killed more than 150 people, mostly children, on February 28 , the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Senior figures at the United Nations have also argued that technologies such as Palantir’s determine the pace and scale at which the Israeli army is able to target people.

HSBC’s fund also purchased $35.7m worth of shares in RTX, among the world’s biggest arms companies, in the first half of this year, the Middle East Eye reported.

RTX Corporation is a US defence company whose businesses include Raytheon, a major manufacturer of missiles, air-defence systems, and military technologies.

Through Raytheon, the corporation partners with the Israeli government-owned Rafael Advanced Defense Systems company to manufacture components and Tamir interceptor missiles for the Iron Dome air-defence system.

Raytheon and the Israeli company also jointly developed David’s Sling, another Israeli missile-defence system. Raytheon also makes Tomahawk missiles and MIM-104 Patriot missile systems for the US military, which have been used in the war on Iran, in addition to providing components to F-series fighter jets that are deployed in the occupied Palestinian territory.

HSBC also invested $20.3m in shares of Analog Devices, a US semiconductor company that has shipped components to Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest privately -owned weapons manufacturer, amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Analog Devices makes electronic components used in surveillance systems, aircraft, and precision-guided munitions.

In July 2025, Irish investigative outlet The Ditch reported that Analog Devices International, the company’s Irish-registered subsidiary, shipped components from its factory in the Philippines to Elbit Systems in August, October and November 2024.

In June 2024, Israel bombed the UN-run al-Sardi school in central Gaza’s Nuseirat refugee camp, killing nearly 40 Palestinians, including at least 14 children and nine women.

A measurement unit from the missile, used to aid with precision targeting, was manufactured by Honeywell, an American conglomerate that specialises in the design and delivery of sensors and guidance devices that are used in a variety of military weapons, an analysis by Al Jazeera had shown .

The HSBC fund purchased $18.9m worth of shares in Honeywell International.

HSBC invested $17.6m in Rolls-Royce Holdings, the only British company identified in the list so far, which manufactures engines and propulsion systems for military aircraft and armoured vehicles.

Its German subsidiary, MTU Aero Engine, has supplied power systems for Israeli military vehicles, including the Merkava tank, Namer armoured personnel carrier, and Eitan armoured vehicle.

In 2023, Rolls-Royce Solutions America received a US military contract to supply power packs for Israel’s Eitan vehicles, with further funding added later. In April 2025, the US approved a potential $180m sale of additional Eitan engines.

How did HSBC’s Sharia fund greenlight weapons firms?

Islamic finance experts explained to Al Jazeera that there are multiple industry standards, at times specific to benchmarks, on what comes under Sharia-compliant funds, especially as they are left to the interpretation of scholars.

“Scholars translate Islamic principles into practical rules within institutions shaped by regulation and commercial pressures,” Jatmiko told Al Jazeera. For example, he pointed out, there are differences between how the S&P and Dow Jones indices identify a Shariah-compliant company. The S&P’s standard Sharia indices do not directly exclude defence companies, whereas the Dow Jones Islamic Market indices exclude them under their screening methods.

Muhammed Ebrahim, a professor of finance at the Business School of Durham University, said there is a “critical gap” in the screening process that assesses the company’s declared principal activities, not the end use of its products or its customers.

“A company classified as ‘technology’ or ‘industrial’ can pass the business activity screen even if its products end up in weapons systems. This is precisely the issue in the HSBC case,” Ebrahim told Al Jazeera. “The screening does not typically trace a company’s supply chain to determine whether its components are used in civilian harm.”

However, an investment can technically be Sharia-compliant, but ethically incompatible with Islamic principles, and “the HSBC case illustrates this gap starkly,” he said.

“The maqaṣid of Islamic law [goals of Islamic doctrine] – including the preservation of life [ḥifẓ al-nafs] and justice [adl] – are not captured by a mechanical sector-exclusion test,” said Ebrahim.

Ebrahim argues that screening should trigger a threshold over any involvement in weapons production or military contracting, review any indirect involvement, and trace the end-use of products.

“The current system does none of these systematically. It relies on sector classification and financial ratios, not supply-chain and end-use analysis,” he said.

HSBC has failed its Muslim customers by investing in Israeli military-linked companies, said Ebrahim.

“The fund is marketed as ‘Sharia-compliant’ to Muslim savers, many of whom hold it through halal pension schemes,” he argued, adding that “those investors reasonably expect that their money is not funding companies implicated in civilian harm.”

Ebrahim and Jatmiko agreed on a core issue: that Islamic finance outsources “ethical judgement to screening providers whose methodologies are opaque and whose definitions are narrow”.

“The HSBC case is a wake-up call: technical compliance is not the same as ethical fidelity,” said Ebrahim. “Funds that invoke the Sharia label have a responsibility to ensure that the substance, not just the form, aligns with the objectives of the law.”

articles.title: Trump backs Netanyahu: Is the US planning a new Iran attack with Israel?
articles.summary: Trump’s endorsement comes after he previously shied away from fully backing Netanyahu’s election campaign.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has announced his official endorsement of Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s election campaign after previously refusing to endorse anyone.

Trump posted on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that Netanyahu had been a “great warrior prime minister and an even greater partner for peace”, adding that Iran had been “systematically destroyed both militarily and financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job.”

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.

“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”.

The president added that normal men and women would have “wilted” under the pressure that Netanyahu was under, but the Israeli prime minister “got stronger”.

“This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel. BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”, he added.

The Israeli election will be on October 27 . According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz’s tracker, as of Sunday, the opposition alliance led by the Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot is expected to win the most seats, at 52, with Netanyahu’s Likud party-led coalition taking 51 of the 120 seats in the Knesset.

So far, no party is projected to secure an outright majority.

But Trump’s endorsement comes after he had previously shied away from fully backing Netanyahu’s election campaign.

Earlier this month, when asked twice by TIME magazine if Netanyahu should be given another term, Trump pivoted to his own popularity in Israel and Washington’s actions supporting Israel.

When asked on Thursday by the right-wing US news outlet, Newsmax, if he was planning to get involved in the Israeli elections, Trump said: “They’d like me to be. Yeah, they’d like me to be”.

When asked whether he trusted Netanyahu, Trump replied, “I don’t trust anybody, honestly”.

Still, Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East North Africa programme at the British think tank Chatham House, explained that Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu was “politically significant” because it comes after months of tension between the two leaders.

“It allows Netanyahu to reinforce his claim that he is indispensable to Israel’s relationship with Washington,” Vakil told Al Jazeera.

“However, its electoral impact should not be overstated. Israeli voters remain divided over Netanyahu’s leadership and the outcome of the Iran war. The endorsement may help consolidate his existing support, but it does not resolve the wider questions surrounding his record,” she added.

Andreas Krieg, senior lecturer at the school of security studies at King’s College London, said that Trump’s endorsement was a “political gift” to Netanyahu, whose electoral campaign is struggling.

But like Vakil, he cautioned against treating Trump’s endorsement as a game-changer.

“Netanyahu’s problems are structural, involving fragmented right-wing parties, disillusioned ultra-Orthodox voters and the legacy of October 7. Trump may mobilise reluctant Likud voters, potentially worth a seat or two in a close contest, but he cannot manufacture the coalition majority Netanyahu currently lacks,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.

What the endorsement means for the Iran war

Much of Trump’s endorsement has been heavily focused on the Iran war, at a time when many analysts suggest the US president might be looking to restart attacks, either before or after the midterm elections in early November.

The conflict, which began in February after the US and Israel launched attacks across Iran, is currently at a standstill.

The Strait of Hormuz, which once transported 20 percent of global crude, was effectively shut by Iran after the war started. A US naval blockade of Iranian vessels followed, as each country struck ships passing through the waterway that they accused of not complying with its orders. Oil traffic last month through the strait picked up to pre-war levels as the US Navy shepherded an increasing number of tankers. But a spate of Iranian attacks on vessels early this month has again hit crude exports through Hormuz.

On Monday morning, Brent crude futures stood at $107.57 a barrel, down slightly after reaching their highest since May 19 on Friday, when they briefly touched $110 a barrel.

Last month, Iran presented a proposal to Washington to reopen the waterway within seven days, but negotiations failed after the US did not address Tehran’s seven conditions, which included the lifting of sanctions and the ending of its naval blockade.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday that the proposal remained on the table and, if Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day.

At the same time, Araghchi, in a post on X on Sunday night, accused Netanyahu of wanting to restart attacks on Iran with the US to “stay out of jail”.

“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” he wrote.

“Netanyahu is driving America into another war to stay out of jail, whatever the consequences for Israel – let alone POTUS,” he added.

Krieg said Trump was prioritising the use of “coercive leverage” through his endorsement of Netanyahu but not necessarily “war over diplomacy”.

“The naval blockade is hurting Iran considerably and Washington believes time is working in its favour. Trump’s calculation is that Iran will eventually accept nuclear concessions and reopen Hormuz, without Washington having to offer significant concessions first,” he argued.

“His endorsement reinforces the military threat underpinning that strategy. But it does not mean diplomacy is finished. Trump still wants a deal he can present as a victory. The danger is that Tehran increasingly believes it must escalate to improve its bargaining position.”

Vakil explained that, while Trump’s declaration of support for Netanyahu had signalled renewed political alignment with Israel and left the door open for future joint military action, it also makes it “harder for Trump to distance himself from the war or portray the US as having been reluctantly drawn into it”.

“He is explicitly taking ownership of the partnership and its military campaign against Iran. However, the endorsement does not necessarily mean that the two leaders have agreed on another operation, nor does it settle the question of who initially pushed hardest for war,” she said.

Vakil added that for Tehran, the statement will reinforce the belief of Iranian leaders that there is “little meaningful distinction between US and Israeli objectives.”

“At the same time, Trump’s suggestion that he is reluctant to confront Iran without Netanyahu could be interpreted as evidence of the limits of Washington’s appetite for another war.”

Meanwhile, while Trump has said that he would not attack Iran before the November midterms, several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before voters head to the polls.

Last week, US news outlet Axios reported, citing both US and Israeli officials, that both Trump and Netanyahu had spoken about launching a major new operation against Iran ahead of the elections in both countries.

For Krieg, the likelihood that the US and Israel launch an attack on Iran remains low, assuming there is no Iranian strike that forces a response.

“The more dangerous window opens after November 3 [US midterms], when those electoral constraints disappear. Both militaries are preparing for that possibility. The greatest immediate risk is an uncontrolled escalation in Hormuz that forces Washington’s hand before either leader is politically ready,” he said.

articles.title: Can religion help Democrats win in red states? These faith leaders hope so
articles.summary: Roughly nine pastors, seminary students and Sunday school teachers are running as Democrats in the US midterm election.
articles.body:
In the landscape of religious life in the United States, Reverend Adam Hamilton has a massive pulpit.

The organisation he founded, the Church of the Resurrection, is considered the largest United Methodist congregation in the country. It spans nine campuses and 23,000 members. Hamilton himself has authored more than 30 books.

But this November, Hamilton is eyeing an even bigger platform: the US Congress.

A mild-mannered pastor with square glasses and a receding swoop of white hair, Hamilton is hoping to achieve what many political observers once dismissed as far-fetched.

He is hoping to win a seat representing Kansas in the US Senate – as a Democrat.

Not since 1932 has a Democrat won a Senate race in the Midwestern state. Kansas is considered ruby red, with a conservative base that leans towards right-wing leaders like President Donald Trump.

But Hamilton is part of a trend in the 2026 midterm election cycle. Largely in right-leaning states, several Christian leaders have stood for election as Democrats, bucking the stereotype that religion is the domain of conservatives.

Approximately nine Democratic faith leaders, seminary students and Sunday school teachers are in the running for federal office in the November 3 election. At least a dozen were on the ballot during the primary elections earlier this year.

Many are competing in states like Iowa, Texas, Arkansas and Tennessee, which have a history of backing right-wing candidates in statewide elections.

Their campaigns have raised questions about whether appealing to Christian voters can be a path to victory for Democrats in the hotly contested midterms.

Reverend Shannon Fleck, executive director of Faithful America, a progressive Christian advocacy organisation, believes some voters have grown disenchanted with the Republican claim on religious values.

Democratic candidates, she argues, can offer an alternative.

"This is going to move the needle even more in red states because, in our homes, faith has been a part of our ecosystem for forever, but it’s also been manipulated by our leaders for forever," Fleck, an Oklahoma resident, said.

She added that faith-inspired Democratic candidates have "more opportunities for turnover" in right-leaning states, "because we are so intimately familiar with the other option".

articles.title: In 2024, a couple bought a neglected 1800s Brooklyn lodging house and uncovered a 1901 coal delivery schedule linked to the husband's family history; after a difficult restoration, it is becoming their third guesthouse
articles.summary: When James and Laureta Gale entered the basement of a run-down 1880s Brooklyn lodging house in 2024, they expected to find damaged walls, dust and old
articles.body: When James and Laureta Gale entered the basement of a run-down 1880s Brooklyn lodging house in 2024, they expected to find damaged walls, dust and old plumbing. Instead, beneath layers of dirt, they found a forgotten piece of history: a handwritten coal delivery schedule from 1901. The discovery had a special meaning for the couple. According to People magazine, James's grandfather had worked as a coal truck driver, bringing fuel from Pennsylvania's Shenandoah Valley to New York City. During that same period, coal was used to heat brownstones and lodging houses across the city's boroughs. James's father was also born in Brooklyn, while his grandmother lived in the area.Laureta recalled the moment the couple realised what was pinned to the basement wall. "When we saw it, it felt surreal," Laureta told People magazine. "It was like uncovering a small piece of the house's story, and somehow a piece of James's family history too." The couple run a small hospitality business called Gale Guesthouses. They bought the neglected 19th-century property in 2024, planning to turn it into their third guesthouse.Structural setbacks and hidden artifactsTurning the abandoned building into a working guesthouse has brought many physical and financial challenges. Built in the late Victorian era, the limestone and brick building was first used as a family home. It was later changed into a lodging house with several rooms before years of neglect left it in poor condition. An early inspection revealed serious structural problems. During the demolition work, contractors found rotten support beams on several floors. In one incident, a brick beam spanning three floors collapsed after being supported by a single weakened post. The couple had to stop construction and carry out urgent work to make the building safe. Along with the structural problems, the property revealed several historic features hidden beneath years of modern changes. According to social media updates and interviews published by People magazine, the restoration team found an original stained-glass pocket door, wallpaper patterns more than 100 years old, hidden woodwork in the entrance area and vintage dress bustles left behind by residents in the late 1800s. To bring the building up to modern standards, the couple also had to fix a major gas line problem. They dug trenches to install new utility lines and fitted energy-efficient heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems. They also added a custom layout for lighting and fog effects.Transforming a historic lodging houseThe 1880s building is being converted into an 11-room guesthouse. Each room will have a small kitchen and an updated private bathroom. The couple worked closely with local experts in historic restoration to preserve the original woodwork, decorative moldings and brickwork while ensuring the building met modern safety and construction rules. The project is the latest addition to Gale Guesthouses. The business focuses on restoring neglected or historic Brooklyn townhouses and turning them into boutique places to stay.James explained that carrying out a full historic renovation in New York City means balancing the need to preserve the past with high operating costs. "It took longer than we thought, and it was harder than we imagined," James said in video updates about the project cited by People magazine. "Sometimes restoring an old building feels less like renovation and more like coming home."A family connection to Brooklyn historyFinding the 1901 coal delivery schedule reminded the couple of how the building was used more than a century ago. At that time, horses filled Brooklyn's unpaved streets, and coal fireplaces were the main source of heat. James's family connection to the neighbourhood's industrial past gave the project a deeper personal meaning. His grandfather was among the delivery workers who used horse-drawn carts and early fuel trucks to carry coal across the East River. They delivered fuel to homes and other residential buildings like the one the couple is now restoring. As work on the upper floors approaches completion, the couple plans to frame and preserve the original 1901 delivery schedule. articles.title: Benny Gantz drops out of Israel’s election race
articles.summary: Decision comes after polls showed his Blue and White party below the 3.25 percent threshold needed to enter the Knesset.
articles.body:
Benny Gantz, a former Israeli army chief and defence minister, has withdrawn from Israel’s election race after polls showed his party falling short of the threshold for entering parliament.

The leader of the Blue and White (Kahol Lavan) party announced on Monday he will not run in the October 27 polls, saying he will “continue to work for unity”.

The 67-year-old is expected to hold a news conference later on Monday.

Opinion polls in the lead-up to next week’s vote had consistently shown Gantz’s party hovering below the 3.25 percent threshold needed to enter the 120-seat Knesset, or Israel’s parliament.

A former main opposition leader, Gantz sat in a national unity government with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from 2020 to 2021.

He also joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet that was formed to oversee Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Gantz quit the emergency cabinet in early June 2024, saying Netanyahu “is preventing us from advancing toward true victory”.

Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said Gantz’s election withdrawal announcement “was not really expected”, but added that many would see it as being “in line with how he’s conducted himself” after entering politics in 2018.

“This is a man who entered into unity governments with leaders – especially Netanyahu – that he expressly opposed,” said Odeh.

Gantz’s message for unity is narrow, Odeh added, as it referred to “a unity government of Zionist parties, so no Palestinian Israeli parties , no non-Zionist parties in the government, even if that means bringing in Netanyahu again”.

Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads is locked in a tight race with a self-styled Zionist opposition alliance heading into the election, according to recent polling, although neither side appears on track to win a parliamentary majority.

Two Arab-led electoral lists representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats and could be critical to any post-election coalition – but both main blocs have ruled out forming a government with them.

Opposition leaders, including Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is seen as a potential prime minister candidate, welcomed Gantz’s decision as “correct” and “responsible”.

Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York, told Al Jazeera Gantz’s exit from the race does not change the playing field as he was not going to have a major impact on the election.

“Electorally, his departure from the political system is completely irrelevant and inconsequential,” he said. “In terms of the politics, it is also inconsequential,” adding that Gantz had lost “a lot of his aura” when he “overstayed his welcome in the Netanyahu government”.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s new security doctrine: Regional strategy or election ploy?
articles.summary: Experts say Netanyahu’s security doctrine and map of regional alliances serve his political ambitions ahead of elections
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled an updated national security doctrine and displayed a map of rival regional alignments, signalling a security approach that prioritises preemptive military action, the expansion of buffer zones, and the pursuit of new regional partnerships.

The document was developed with the assistance of Israel’s National Security Council and published by the Prime Minister’s Office on Sunday, just nine days before Israel’s parliamentary elections that could spell the end of Netanyahu’s time in office. It outlines a formal policy of preventing perceived threats through military action rather than containment – a policy that has already been seen in action over the past few years, as Israel pursues multiple wars and attacks on its neighbours.

The timing of the map’s release carries particular political significance, with Netanyahu fighting to retain power amid criticism of his conduct in power, the ongoing corruption trial he faces and his handling of the October 7, 2023, attacks, as well as the wars that followed.

As the October 27 election day draws closer, Netanyahu is attempting to bolster his credentials as Israel’s ‘Mr Security’, hoping to get the votes of Israelis who may not like some of his other policies or behaviour, but still view him as the most likely leader to defend the country.

Netanyahu, who did get the endorsement of US President Donald Trump on Sunday , said during the briefing that Israel could face the possibility of a far less supportive administration in Washington in two years, after the end of the Trump presidency.

“In two years, a president… who is extremely hostile to Israel could come to power [in the United States],” Netanyahu warned.

He therefore argued that Israel must “expand our network of alliances and develop capabilities that make us a valuable asset” to other countries as a way of protecting itself if US policy towards it changed.

The comments, according to analysts, suggest that Netanyahu is seeking to portray his leadership as essential to navigating both Israel’s regional military challenges and its diplomatic isolation, all while keeping a fearful electorate reassured.

Mohanad Hage Ali, deputy director for research at the Malcolm H Kerr Carnegie Middle East Center, explained that the strategic presentation centred on competing regional blocs and buffer zones.

That framework “incubates and nurtures existential fears, which would lead Israeli voters to feel the need for a decisive leader”, Hage Ali noted.

In his assessment, Netanyahu stands to benefit from the Israeli public’s fear of regional threats by presenting himself as a familiar leader capable of managing them, making him “the devil you know”, as the analyst put it, to voters reluctant to embrace political change at a sensitive time.

Netanyahu’s political opponents have been quick to push back against that narrative.

Gadi Eisenkot, one of the prime minister’s main challengers in the upcoming election, said that the published doctrine was “two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing to do with a security concept”.

Another, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, described the document as “superficial”.

The map displayed during Netanyahu’s briefing was originally published in May by Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, a German political foundation. It divides the Middle East and parts of Africa into competing blocs, highlighting the region’s complex network of alliances and rivalries.

Those networks include states, unrecognised entities and non-state actors.

The map identifies an Israel-United Arab Emirates alignment, described as the “Hexagon Alliance”, alongside a separate grouping of Egypt, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia – the latter three of which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August – labelled the “Sunni Diamond Alliance”. It also depicts Iran and its regional allies as a separate axis.

The map serves to illustrate the issues outlined in the published security doctrine, presenting a region where Israel faces multiple threats, the alliance that Israel is seeking to cultivate across the wider region, and the perceived need for “buffer zones” – the occupation of territory in other countries.

Israel’s existing illegal occupation of territory in Gaza and southern Lebanon illustrates the potential consequences of expanding the buffer zone approach.

Hage Ali warned that continuing to pursue an approach built around expanding military control could lead to “more conflict and more ethnic cleansing” under the guise of security buffers.

A striking element of the map displayed by Netanyahu is its explicit designation of non-state actors as friendly entities.

The map highlights territories controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan and Khalifa Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army within an alignment deemed cooperative to Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

Israel views these actors as pragmatic partners or at least cooperative entities in a broader strategic grid, Hage Ali explained. However, the public association of these groups with Israel threatens to damage their domestic standing across the Arab world.

That reflects Netanyahu’s immediate priorities, where “what Israelis think matters more than the reputation of your allies and the viability of these alliances”, Hage Ali added.

The portrayal of the Middle East as a region divided into competing alliances also carries risks for Netanyahu’s broader diplomatic ambitions.

Earlier this year, Netanyahu proposed a “hexagon of alliances” , envisaging cooperation between Israel, India, Greece, Cyprus and unnamed Arab, African and Asian partners, against what he described as “radical” regional alliances.

The proposed grouping has not been established as a formal alliance, and commentators in Israel and the international press have described the project as a branding exercise rather than a binding military pact, noting that countries like India prioritise non-alignment and pragmatic trade over ideologically rigid blocs.

For Tehran and its regional partners, the map also offers potent political leverage.

Hage Ali emphasised that the visual layout “will certainly help their propaganda machine”, providing Hezbollah and other Iranian allies with evidence to reinforce the narrative that Israel seeks to expand and dominate the region.

articles.title: London Museum is preparing to open inside historic Smithfield Market after an £437 million redevelopment that took 11 years to reach its launch date
articles.summary: For years, the future of Smithfield’s old market buildings has been tied to a larger question about how London preserves its past while finding new uses
articles.body: For years, the future of Smithfield’s old market buildings has been tied to a larger question about how London preserves its past while finding new uses for its historic spaces. Now, one of the City’s best-known Victorian market halls is being prepared for a different kind of public life. The London Museum is moving into the restored General Market in Farringdon, bringing its collections into a building once associated with the capital’s wholesale meat trade. As reported by London Evening Standard, the redevelopment has taken years of planning and construction, with the budget reaching £437 million. Its opening also marks a new chapter for a museum which is set to open on November 28, 2026, that has spent nearly five decades documenting the changing character of the city.London Museum prepares to expand across Smithfield’s historic market buildingsThe new museum occupies the former General Market building at Smithfield, a site whose working history stretches back far beyond the present redevelopment. The move follows the closure of the museum’s previous premises at London Wall in 2022. Its new home gives the institution an opportunity to present its collections within a different part of the capital, surrounded by buildings that have long been associated with London’s commercial life.The London Museum first opened in December 1976, bringing together objects and accounts that trace the city’s development across centuries. Its relocation comes as the institution approaches its 50th anniversary. The Smithfield site is intended to accommodate a broader presentation of London’s history, with exhibition spaces designed to connect historical objects with the experiences of people living in the city today.Reportedly, the neighbouring Poultry Market, a building dating from the 1960s, is scheduled to become part of the museum complex in 2028. Plans for that phase include further exhibition space, a learning centre and facilities for storing the museum’s collections.Inside the £437 million project to transform Smithfield MarketThe decision to move the museum to Smithfield was confirmed by the City of London Corporation in 2015, following earlier discussions about finding a new home. The original timetable envisaged an opening in 2021, but the work took longer than anticipated as the project dealt with the practical demands of adapting an existing historic structure.Renovating an old market hall presented challenges that would not arise in the same way with a purpose-built museum. The discovery of a freshwater spring beneath the site in August 2022 added another complication to the work. By the time the project approached its launch, the reported cost had risen to £437 million.Funding has come through a partnership involving the City of London Corporation, the Mayor of London and charitable organisations. Supporters include the National Lottery Heritage Fund, the Goldsmiths’ Foundation and the Linbury Trust. The scale of the investment reflects the ambition to preserve the historic building while adapting it for exhibitions, public programmes and other museum activities.What visitors will see inside the museumThe museum’s displays are arranged around three connected areas: Real Time, Our Time and Past Time. Together, they are intended to explore London’s history through objects, personal stories and events that have shaped the capital, rather than presenting its development as a single, uninterrupted timeline.Visitors can expect to encounter material from Roman London, alongside displays relating to events such as the Great Fire of London and the 2012 Olympic Games. Contemporary installations will bring more recent experiences into the galleries, including large animated screens featuring stories from Londoners. Works by modern artists, including Banksy, are also part of the planned offering.The Our Time galleries will focus on the city’s living memory through a series of installations. Among the objects expected to feature are the Lord Mayor’s Coach and Syd’s Coffee Stall, associated with the East End. These displays place familiar aspects of London life alongside items that have survived from earlier periods, giving visitors different ways to understand how neighbourhoods and traditions have changed.A dedicated gallery will house the Cheapside Hoard, a collection of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewellery considered significant for what it reveals about craftsmanship and the trade in precious objects during the period. The new building will also provide a view of the Thameslink railway through a six-metre window, bringing one of Farringdon’s busiest transport routes into the visitor experience.Free admission and events beyond the galleriesGeneral admission to the Smithfield museum is free, following the approach taken at its Docklands branch, which will continue operating as a long-term venue. Separate exhibitions and special experiences may carry additional charges, so visitors will need to check the arrangements for individual events. The museum is also planning activities that extend beyond conventional gallery visits. Proposed programmes include a weekly tea club, late-night DJ sets and monthly dinner clubs. Such events will give the building uses beyond its exhibition spaces, particularly during evenings when visitors might otherwise associate museums with closing time.Food will feature in the programme, too. The London Tastes exhibition is being developed with support from Sainsbury’s and curated by food writer Jonathan Nunn and former Great British Bake Off contestant Ruby Tandoh. Its focus is London’s varied food culture, reflecting the influence of the communities that have shaped the city’s eating habits. Opening hours were yet to be confirmed in the Evening Standard report, so visitors should check the museum’s official channels before making plans. Free general admission does not necessarily mean every event or exhibition will be available without a separate ticket.Smithfield’s long history continues around the museumSmithfield has served London for more than 800 years, with its history closely connected to markets and the movement of food through the capital. The wholesale meat market became a familiar part of the city’s commercial infrastructure, supplying butchers, restaurants and caterers. Its overnight trading schedule has long distinguished it from many other public markets.The museum’s arrival will not mean the wholesale market disappears immediately. Parts of the wider complex will continue to serve their existing purposes while redevelopment proceeds. However, traders have been told they must leave the premises by 2028, as plans move forward to transfer the wholesale meat market and Billingsgate fish market to new facilities in the Royal Docks.The change at Smithfield therefore extends beyond the museum itself. A building that once formed part of London’s working market infrastructure is being adapted to tell the story of the city, while the future of the surrounding market operations is being reshaped elsewhere.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Coming out coach' charges women hundreds for support navigating late in life lesbian transitions
articles.summary: "Coming out coach" Anne-Marie Zanzal charges $400 for a 16-week online program guiding women through identity transitions and support groups.
articles.body: After decades of marriage and motherhood, some middle-aged women are spending hundreds of dollars to join online lesbian support groups led by a "coming out coach" to guide them through the process of coming out late in life, according to a New York Times report. Coming out coach Anne-Marie Zanzal charges $400 for a private online membership designed to help "late-blooming" women, some of whom are still married to their longtime husbands, navigate what she calls "sexual identity transitions." "She helped me see that leaving my marriage wasn’t selfish. It was honest. And my kids are better for it," a testimonial from Zanzal’s website reads. Zanzal also offers a separate 16-week program called "This Authentic Life," which includes live group coaching, individual coaching and access to her "Authentically Us" online community. RELATIONSHIP EXPERT CHALLENGES ONE OF AMERICA'S BIGGEST ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT DIVORCE According to Zanzal’s website, the program helps LGBTQ+ women unpack heavy questions regarding their sexuality alongside others navigating similar experiences. "It is not too late, and you are not too late. Come as you are, and let us walk this part of the road together," Zanzal’s website reads. "We were looking for women who came to this the way we did, later in life and carrying a whole history, who would never ask us to explain any of it." Zanzal, who holds a master's degree in divinity from Yale Divinity School, began her "coming out coaching" business in 2018. She came out at age 52 after being married to a man for nearly 30 years and raising four children with him. "I help women come home to themselves — with clarity, self-kindness, and community — so they can live authentically without abandoning the lives and relationships that matter to them," Zanzal writes on her coaching site. "That is why I built this work. Not because I have a degree in it — though I do … But because I lived it, in the dark, for a very long time." PARENTS DROP EYE POPPING FEES ON SORORITY RUSH COACHES TO GET KIDS INTO ELITE COLLEGE GREEK LIFE During the support meetings, women share personal updates with the group and their coming-out coach. One woman, for example, discussed preparing to tell her son that she was a lesbian over a beer, according to a profile of Zanzal's business published in the Times on Wednesday. In an interview with the outlet, one of Zanzal’s clients named Shelly said she worried that coming out to her family would upend her "perfectly good" dynamic. Shelly said Zanzal helped her understand that any unhappiness her children felt about her sexuality transition was "likely to fade with time and be only a part of their story," whereas, her own pain could be permanent if she continued to conceal her identity. Podcast host Ben Ferguson told Fox News Digital he found the messages being sent to women through this coaching service "outrageous." "What’s especially outrageous is the suggestion that a mother’s unhappiness is permanent, but her children’s pain will somehow just fade away," Ferguson said in a statement. "Children aren’t disposable characters in their parents’ journey of self-discovery. Marriage involves commitment, and parenting requires sacrifice," he added. GROWING TREND OF HATING MEN BACKFIRES AS ANTI-MARRIAGE CULTURE LEAVES SINGLE WOMEN LOSING OUT Ferguson argued that the business model — which includes $150 one-hour "clarity calls" with a coming out coach and $77 self-paced courses, including the "Maybe I am Not Straight Course" — is "deeply disturbing" and appears to monetize women’s personal struggles. "This isn’t about being gay or straight," he said. "It’s about charging people hundreds of dollars to navigate decisions that could tear their families apart, with seemingly zero accountability for the damage left behind. That’s not compassion or empowerment. That’s opportunism disguised as counseling." Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff offered a different perspective, arguing that Zanzal’s "community-driven" coming-out coaching reflects a broader cultural shift in how people seek support. "There is so much more freedom and language around sexuality and what makes a modern relationship that it isn’t surprising older women are looking at that and realizing they never had space to ask some of these deep questions of themselves," he told Fox News Digital. Just 1% of LGBTQ+ women come out at 50 or older, according to a 2024 Gallup survey, and the number of teenage girls identifying as lesbian or bisexual has plunged in the last four years, a new study reveals.
